text: Today's lab works through one real, messy scenario combining the last two lessons: an enterprise with twelve separate point-to-point integrations between ServiceNow and its HR system, built over six years, with no central documentation and inconsistent authentication.

No inventory exists. Five of the twelve integrations authenticate with OAuth, four with Basic Auth, and three still use an API key issued when the connection was first built and never rotated since. All twelve currently use request-response. As the technical architect, your first job isn't to fix anything yet — it's to find out what actually exists.

Step one is building the integration inventory: interviewing each owning team, inspecting the actual REST Message and IntegrationHub configurations, and recording purpose, direction, authentication, and owner for every integration. Doing this alone surfaces a real problem — integrations three and nine turn out to both pull organizational-chart data independently, built two years apart by teams that never knew about each other.

Step two sets one enterprise authentication standard: OAuth for every HR integration. The five already on OAuth stay put. The four on Basic Auth get migrated. The three on the unrotated API key move first, because a long-lived, never-rotated credential is the highest standing security risk in the whole inventory. The duplicate org-chart integrations get merged, taking the count from twelve down to eleven.

Step three asks which integration pattern fits which volume. Ten of the eleven remaining integrations are low-volume and correctly stay request-response. The new-hire record sync is different: its volume has roughly tripled with the company, and the business confirms ServiceNow doesn't need an immediate answer back. That's the real case for moving it to event-driven — with the honest cost of now handling possible duplicate event delivery and building monitoring for anything missed.

That's a complete architectural recommendation: an inventory covering every integration, one consistent OAuth standard prioritized by actual security risk, and a pattern decision driven by real volume rather than preference. Chapter 5 starts next, on the architectural tradeoffs behind enterprise security decisions.
